recovering-a-registry-command.text: You run singular registry create, open-datum insert, open-datum update, open-datum terminate or inspect (singular registry inspect or open-datum inspect), and something goes wrong between your machine and the chain: the node's answer to a submission never arrives, the process is killed, the machine stops halfway through saving its files, or a transaction the chain had included is rolled back. You want to know which of those happened, you want the next command to pick up from where the last one stopped without sending anything twice, and you want to be told plainly when it cannot.

This page describes what the ordinary commands do in each case and what you do next. Every write records each transaction it submits in the registry's journal, journal.jsonl, phase by phase, before taking the next step: prepared (the signed body saved beside the journal, before it is sent), the node's answer, the confirmation, and observed (what the transaction made, read back from the chain). A fold's prepared line lists every request it folds, one transition per request, chained from the root before to the root after. The journal is only ever appended to; saved bodies are never rewritten.

the-request-keeps-its-registrys-windows.text: The request keeps its registry's windows.

As a requester recovering after an interruption, you read processTime and retractTime from registry inspect to see the windows stored in the live state datum. They were chosen once at registry create with --process-time and --retract-time, or defaulted to 600 000 and 300 000 milliseconds (ten and five minutes). Both are fixed for the life of the registry; restarting a command or reconciling its journal does not restart or extend a request's windows. A booking's fold deadline remains its submission time plus the registry's processing window, followed by the owner's retract window.

the-case-each-submission-met.text: Every write's receipt lists the transactions it prepared under submissions, each with its step, its id, its case and whether its after-state was observed. The case is read from the latest phase the journal holds for the transaction:

A command that stops after a submission exits partial (status 15), or timeout (13) when the confirmation deadline passed, and its receipt names the case. Nothing is ever sent a second time: a transaction is prepared once, and the journal shows exactly one prepared line for it.

the-next-command-reconciles.text: After an inclusion, the command selects its proof state from public state-token history and reads back the step's after-state before appending observed. For a fold of several requests, it reads back every key the fold touches and the registry's state output carrying the last transition's root after. The next ordinary write or inspect reconciles unfinished observations from public chain evidence before proceeding, without submitting anything. Proof state is reconstructed afresh; no mirror or saved-root file is read or written.

The journal tracks this actor's submissions. It never supplies a replay edge, proof or root. Missing history and a root that does not chain are named refusals; an empty trie cannot substitute for unavailable history. The observation concerns every key the interrupted step touched, even when the current command targets another key: for a fold, every key its transitions name and the registry's state output.

A write reports reconciliation under reconciled: rolledBack, recovery, excluded and observed. Inspect reports the same fields at the receipt's top level. Inspect reconciles only while no other process holds this directory's write lock; otherwise it reads without reconciling and says so.

when-the-chain-rolls-back.text: A transaction journalled confirmed or observed can leave the chain again. The next command checks every such transaction against the chain it reads: when its first output is not live and an input it spends is live again, it is no longer on the chain, since a transaction on the chain has consumed every input it spends. The command appends a rolled-back line naming the chain point it read and the inputs it found live; for a fold, the line names that its requests are pending again and the public state returns to its root before. The observed line it supersedes stays where it was.

Proof state follows the public history selected by the current command, including rollbacks. The journal does not rebuild a private trie. The rolled-back transaction is never sent again. If the chain includes it again, the next command journals it confirmed and reconciles its observation; otherwise writes stop on it, naming the case rolled-back.

when-a-transaction-can-never-land.text: When a transaction can never land.

A transaction carries a validity window. Once the chain's tip has reached the end of that window and an input the transaction spends is still live — so it is not on the chain — it can never be included. The next command appends an excluded line naming the chain point it read and the live inputs. The transaction is settled in the journal: no later command stops on it, and its edge was never applied. A write that excluded a transaction then proceeds, building from the root selected by fresh public replay.

What the excluded transaction leaves on chain depends on the command. An excluded update leaves nothing: run it again. The fold of an insert or a terminate is the second of two transactions, and the first, its booking, is on chain: its request stays pending, holding its deposit. Use registry fold while its processing window allows it, or registry reclaim with the owner's wallet in its retract window. After both windows expire the request stays pending: registry reject, which once cleared it, is retired. An insertion's request carries its envelope on chain. A folder reads it publicly and reconstructs proofs from history; neither an insertion fold nor a termination fold needs the booker's files.

A fold carries an upper bound on its validity window. A booking, and the publications create makes, carry none: a booking that never landed, or one rolled back and not included again, stays unresolved however far the chain moves on, and every write stops on it. That is a known limit of these commands, not a judgement about the transaction.

when-a-bundle-waits-for-signatures.text: When a bundle waits for signatures.

As Bob, I ran a write naming my address and a bundle file, or Alice ran one from her vault, and I want to know where its bundle stands: still waiting for signatures, landed, or dead. The next write in the same state directory tells me, before it builds anything. The bundle's transactions are judged by one thing only: whether the chain holds their identities. Their outputs, their inputs and the after-state of the registry do not count. A transaction of a bundle is its member for its whole life.

Pending. Some member is not on chain yet, and the tip has not reached any member's deadline. The next write stops before it builds anything, with status 19, waiting-for-signatures, naming the bundle's hash, its saved path, and the members awaited with their deadlines.
Landed. Every member is found on chain. Each gets a landed line with its chain point and confirmations. The next write builds normally, and its receipt reports the bundle under reconciled.
Dead. A member can never land. Every member not landed gets a dead line, and the report names the members that went through. The next write builds normally.
A bundle dies one of these ways, and the dead line says which:

A pending bundle never needs the journal edited. Sign the bundle and send it with singular submit, or let a member's deadline pass and run the command again. A vault run whose answer from the node was lost ends partial, and the next write settles its bundle by identity in the same way. A write that sent its transactions and then could not journal the outcome keeps the submission's outcome and its sends in the receipt, and names what failed on its own.

A bundle sent elsewhere and refused by the node is not seen by your journal, since singular submit keeps no state: it dies when a member's deadline passes. A create bundle has no deadline, so it stays pending. As Alice, if my co-signer never signs the create bundle I staged, or it is refused when sent elsewhere, I correct the cause and send it again. A create from the same wallet without --seed picks the same output again while that output is unspent, so it is stopped at 19 too. The way out is a create that names another output with --seed: a different registry, in a different state directory, which nothing blocks. The pending create's journal stays as a record and blocks nothing else.

when-the-next-command-stops.text: A write that finds a transaction it cannot reconcile stops before it builds or submits anything. Its outcome is partial (status 15), and its receipt names the transaction under unresolved with its step, its last journalled phase and its case; the journal does not move.

acknowledged, unknown or timeout: the chain does not yet show the transaction. Wait for the network and run the command again; when the transaction lands, the next command reconciles it, and when its validity window closes without it, the next command excludes it — for the fold of an insert or a terminate, with the pending request it leaves.

rolled-back: the chain no longer shows a transaction it had included. Wait and run the command again; it reconciles the transaction if the chain includes it again, and excludes it once its validity window closes without it, with the same pending request when it is a fold. A booking has no window and stays rolled back.

included: the transaction is on chain, but public history is incomplete or its reconstructed root does not chain. The named trie refusal preserves its existing outcome and exit status; the journal cannot repair public facts.
inspect names the same unresolved transaction and its case, with the outcome partial, alongside the root and chain point it read.

what-the-checks-show.text: The recovery controls run each hosted partition as separate singular processes against its own generated development node, and judge every clause from the receipts the processes printed, the registry's journal, its saved bodies and its files, and — for exclusion and rollback — from the node's own answers, read with devnet probe and its block adoption trace, never through the command under test. The partitions are listed in one place in the root flake; the discovery command prints them for the workflow matrix, and each partition runs by key:

The combined .#cli-recovery-controls command is retired: it serialised every part on one node and exceeded the receipt cap of 52428800 bytes before reaching never-sent and rollback. The per-partition commands above are generated from the same partition list the workflow matrix uses.

The rolled-back control is a mechanism of the generated development node — its database restored to an earlier copy — and not a fork of a public chain: it shows what the commands do when the chain they read no longer holds a transaction, not how often or how deeply a public network rolls back. Across every control, each journalled transaction has exactly one prepared line, the journal is only ever appended to, and no saved body changes. These controls do not establish durability across a power loss, only across a killed process.
